meaning: She of the womb. The planet Venus as deity. Queen of heaven.

phonemes.desc: Glottal stop [ʔ] plus open [a]; the name may also have begun with a pharyngeal in some dialects.
Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] plus t; the š is written with a caron (š) to distinguish it from plain s.
Long [aː] followed by r and final t; the -t is a feminine ending, perhaps originally a nominal suffix.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ash-TART' or 'ASH-tart' — with a crisp 'sh' and a drawn-out second syllable; the final t is pronounced.

pronunciation.note: Aštart is a Tier-1 name: it preserves the distinctive š (postalveolar fricative) via a caron — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The long ā in the second syllable is marked by macron in scholarly transcription; the name's Greek-influenced doublet, Astartē, is not used as the primary form because the project owns Aštart.

domains.title: She of the Womb, Queen of Heaven
domains.subtitle: Love, War, Fertility, and the Morning Star
domains.lead: Aštart is the Phoenician Venus — a goddess in whom love and war are not opposites but twin faces of the same radiant power. She is 'she of the womb,' the planet Venus as deity, and the Queen of Heaven invoked by women across the Levant. In Ugarit she stands just behind ꜥAnat in the warrior-huntress pair; in Phoenicia and Egypt she becomes one of the most widely traveled goddesses of antiquity.

cards.name: Venus and the Stars
cards.desc: The morning and evening star; her celestial body marks the boundaries between day and night, human and divine.

cards.name: Love and Desirability
cards.desc: She governs sexual attraction, fertility, and the life-giving power of the womb; her cult emphasized renewal.

cards.name: Warrior and Huntress
cards.desc: KTU 1.92 casts her as a huntress in the wilderness; in Egypt she rides chariots and battles enemies beside the king.

cards.name: Queen of Heaven
cards.desc: The title invoked by Jewish women in Egypt (Jeremiah 44) and by Phoenician devotees across the Mediterranean.

mythology.lead: Aštart's mythology is more dispersed than centralized. She appears in Ugaritic texts as a huntress and member of Ēl's household, but her full fame comes from Phoenician, Egyptian, and later Greco-Roman cult. She is the goddess who crosses borders as easily as the Phoenician ships that carried her.

myths.title: Aštart the Huntress
myths.text: KTU 1.92 is the only Ugaritic literary text in which Aštart is the protagonist, and it is short and partly broken. The goddess arms herself and goes out into the šd, the open country, where she hunts and fells game; she then returns to serve the meat at the table of her father Ēl and of Yarikh, the moon god. Johannes de Moor's edition titled it Athtartu the Huntress, and it remains the clearest window on her Ugaritic personality — not yet the queen of a great city cult, as she would become at Sidon, but a divine huntress of the wilderness, a goddess of the between places where game runs and boundaries blur. The text has been connected with the ritual hunt known from Emar on the Euphrates, suggesting a seasonal rite lay behind the poem. Even in fragments the figure is vivid: the armed maiden of the steppe, bringing home the kill for the high god's table.

myths.title: In the Household of Ēl
myths.text: In KTU 1.114 — the tale of Ēl's drunken banquet — Aštart appears at the high god's table alongside ꜥAnat, her constant companion in the Ugaritic sources. The two goddesses are the most animated members of Ēl's household: they feast, they stagger home with the incapacitated father of gods, and they share his appetite and his lack of ceremony. The scene is comic, but the pairing is theologically pointed. Where later traditions split the dangerous feminine into separate deities — a love goddess here, a war goddess there — Ugarit kept Aštart and ꜥAnat together as sister powers, appetite and ferocity dining at the same table. Both are called btlt, 'maiden'; both refuse the settled roles of wife and mother. The household of Ēl — the Bible's arch-foe — is here simply a family: loud, tipsy, and fond of its unruly daughters.

myths.title: Queen of Heaven
myths.text: Aštart's Phoenician career turned her into a civic sovereign. At Sidon she presided over one of the Levant's greatest sanctuaries, honored in royal inscriptions from the ninth century onward; at Tyre she stood beside Melqart as the city's divine pair. Her title Queen of Heaven — mlkt šmym — became so beloved that it outlived her cult: in Jeremiah 44, Jewish refugees in Egypt tell the prophet to his face that their wives, daughters, and they themselves have kept baking cakes for the Queen of Heaven, 'as we and our ancestors... did in the towns of Judah.' Farther west, the gold tablets of Pyrgi record a joint dedication of the Caeretan sanctuary to Uni — usually identified with Aštart — and the local king. Her cult traveled Phoenician trade routes from Carthage to Kition to Sicily, making her one of the most widely worshipped goddesses of the first millennium BCE.

myths.title: The Warrior of the Nile
myths.text: New Kingdom Egypt adopted the Levantine goddess with enthusiasm. From the reign of Amenhotep II onward, Aštart — ꜥa-set-ir-ti — appears as a goddess of horses and chariotry, shown with the naked body, Hathoric wig, and raised scimitar of the Asiatic war goddess, protecting the pharaoh in his chariot and trampling his enemies. At Tanis and Memphis her cult flourished; Ramesside tradition could identify her with the leonine Sakhmet, and her image spreads across Delta scarabs and temple reliefs. A late Egyptian tale — the so-called Astarte Papyrus, its leading women nameless in what survives — dramatizes the Sea's demand for tribute from the gods, a plot scholars have long compared with the Ugaritic Baꜥal Cycle; whether Aštart stood at its center is debated. Either way, the papyrus shows how deeply her mythic world had been naturalized on the Nile by the end of the Bronze Age.

lore.syncretism: Aštart is the West Semitic face of the older Mesopotamian Ištar, and the two names almost certainly share a common ancestor, though the exact historical path is debated. The Greeks identified her with Aphrodítē in matters of love and with Ártemis in matters of hunting; the Romans made her their Venus. In Egypt she merged with Sakhmet and Hathor. Some scholars trace her imagery forward into the figure of the Virgin Mary (the Queen of Heaven) and even into the Christian iconography of the dove. She is, in short, one of the great transformers of ancient Mediterranean religion.
lore.culturalLegacy: Aštart's name survives in the biblical ʿAštōreth — deliberately vocalized to echo bōšet, 'shame' — and her title Queen of Heaven echoes whenever Jeremiah's refugees are read aloud. The oft-repeated claim that the Christian feast of Easter took its name from her has no scholarly standing: Bede himself derives English Ēostre from a Germanic dawn goddess, and the Romance languages name the feast from Hebrew Pesaḥ (Pâques, Pascua). What is certain is that Aštart was among the most widely worshipped goddesses of the first millennium BCE, carried by Phoenician ships from Carthage to Cyprus to Sicily; her temples, doves, lions, and naked-warrior image long outlived the city-states that raised them. In modern Neopaganism she returns as a goddess of sacred sexuality, warriorship, and the morning star.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Aštart refuses to be one thing. She is the morning star and the evening star, the womb and the battlefield, the naked goddess and the armored charioteer. Where later traditions split these powers among separate deities, she held them together, and her very multiplicity made her portable across cultures.

To sit with Aštart is to sit with the ancient intuition that creation and destruction are not enemies. The same desire that brings lovers together can drive armies apart; the same planet that heralds dawn also marks the threshold of night. She is the goddess of thresholds, and her cult was always strongest wherever two worlds met — sea and land, East and West, mortal and divine.
lore.originalScriptNote: Ugaritic writes the name 𐎓𐎘𐎚𐎗𐎚 (ʿ-ṯ-t-r-t, ʿṯtrt), the five-sign spelling attested in KTU 1.92; 𐎀𐎘𐎗𐎚 (ʾaṯrt) is Asherah's name, not hers. Phoenician writes 𐤀𐤔𐤕𐤓𐤕 (ʾ-š-t-r-t). The middle consonant is a voiceless postalveolar fricative, transliterated š. The PUNICODEX primary form Aštart uses the Latin š with caron (U+0161) to mark this sound, avoiding the Hellenized doublet Astartē.

sources.name: Pardee, Ritual and Cult at Ugarit

lore.archaeology: Ugaritic KTU 1.92 casts her as a huntress in alphabetic cuneiform, while Phoenician inscriptions from Sidon, Tyre, Kition, and the Carthage tophet invoke her as a civic and funerary goddess. In Egypt, New Kingdom reliefs and statuettes from Tanis, Memphis, and Pi-Ramesses present her as a chariot warrior and horse goddess. The Pyrgi gold tablets record a joint dedication to Uni/Aštart, and the Karatepe bilingual names her alongside Baʿal.
